# Introducing the Idea

A quick post about an idea that has proven useful in teaching statistics.

```{r}

library(ggplot2) # dummy call to ggplot

```

```{css, echo = FALSE}

.math.display .MathJax {
  font-size: 300% !important;
}

```

$$\text{\color{purple}{Data}} = \text{\color{blue}{Model}} + \text{\color{red}{Error}}$$ {#eq-data-equals-model-plus-error}

I have no clear memory of where I first heard this phrase, but I have an idea that it was in the blog of [https://www.johndcook.com/](https://www.johndcook.com/).

The idea, as I have understood it, is that our [**observed data about the real world**]{fg="#800080"}, can be broken down into two parts: [**our model of the world**]{fg="#0000FF"}; and [**the ways in which our model is wrong**]{fg="#FF0000"}.

Consider a basic regression equation:

$$\color{purple}{y_i} \color{black}{=} \color{blue}{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i}} \color{black}{+} \color{red}{e_i}$$ {#eq-basic-regression-equation}

Broadly speaking, as we add independent variables (e.g. $x_2, x_3, \text{etc}...$) to the [**model**]{fg="#0000FF"} we reduce the amount of variation in $y_i$ that needs to be explained by the [**error**]{fg="#FF0000"}, $e_i$:  as the model gains more power, the error decreases.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Specific Implications for Multilevel Models

This idea has specific implications for multilevel models, because multilevel models divide up the [**error**]{fg="#FF0000"} into pieces. For example $e_{ij}$ may become $e_{ij} + u_{0j}$. As the $x$'s in the model start to explain more and more of the variation in the dependent variable $y_{ij}$, the random intercept $u_{0j}$, possibly along with other random effects, often becomes less and less significant, and may ultimately become an *insignificant* part of the model. Put more intuitively: sometimes one starts with an unconditional multilevel model in which the random effects are a statistically significant part; as more and more $x$'s are added to the model, the random effects (e.g. $u_{0j}$) become less and less important and may even become statistically insignificant! As we improve the multilevel model, the multilevel aspect of the model may become unnecessary!
:::

# "All Models Are Wrong, Some Are Useful"

I am perennially thinking about George Box's idea that "all models are wrong, and some are useful" [@Box1979]. Box's idea seems to have some connections to the idea that $\text{\color{purple}{Data}} = \text{\color{blue}{Model}} + \text{\color{red}{Error}}$. As we add independent variables to our model, we are essentially trying to make our model less wrong. Models are abstractions of reality, so no model is a perfect accounting of reality, but we can always test our models against the data. And we can test whether a more complex model is less wrong than a simpler model. 

# A Map of the World

I also connect Box's idea, and the idea of $\text{\color{purple}{Data}} = \text{\color{blue}{Model}} + \text{\color{red}{Error}}$ to Borges' [-@Borges] story of the map-maker. Briefly, the map-maker tried to make as accurate a map of the world as they could. But this perfectly accurate map turned out to be as large as the world itself, and therefore of little use. To be useful, a map has to be an abstraction, it has to be smaller than the world that it tries to describe.
